title: Kill Process
statement:
There are `n` running processes, described by two arrays of length `n`: process `i` has the ID `pid[i]`, and `ppid[i]` is the ID of its parent process. Exactly one process is the root and has `ppid[i] = 0`; every other process has exactly one parent, and together they form a single rooted tree. All IDs in `pid` are distinct.

Stopping a process also stops all of its children, their children, and so on down the tree. Given the ID `kill` of the process you stop, return the IDs of every process that ends up stopped, `kill` included. The IDs may be listed in any order. `kill` is always one of the IDs in `pid`.
constraints: All values of pid are unique
The processes form one rooted tree
kill is one of the values in pid
signature: List<Integer> killProcess(List<Integer> pid, List<Integer> ppid, int kill)
notes:
## Intuition

The input says who each process's parent is, but stopping a process spreads downwards, to its children. So first flip the parent links into lists of children, keyed by parent ID. Then the stopped processes are exactly the subtree under `kill`, which a depth-first search from `kill` collects. A slower idea is to climb from every process towards the root and see whether `kill` is on the way, which can cost O(n²) on a long chain.

## Approach

1. Build `children`: a map from each parent ID to the list of its child IDs, in one pass over `pid` and `ppid`.
2. Start a `stack` holding only `kill`, and an empty list `killed`.
3. While the stack is not empty, pop a process `current` and add it to `killed`.
4. Push each of its children from `children` (none for a leaf) so they are stopped too.
5. When the stack is empty, `killed` holds the whole subtree; return it.

## Example 1, step by step

`pid = [1,3,10,5]`, `ppid = [3,0,5,3]`, `kill = 5`. The map is `3 → [1, 5]`, `0 → [3]`, `5 → [10]`.

- `stack = [5]`: pop `5`, `killed = [5]`, push its child `10`.
- `stack = [10]`: pop `10`, `killed = [5, 10]`; `10` has no children.
- The stack is empty, so the answer is `[5, 10]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): building the map touches each process once, and the search pops each stopped process once.
- Space: O(n) for the map, the stack and the result.

## Pitfalls

- Searching up the parent links from `kill` finds its ancestors, which are not stopped; the search must go down.
- A leaf has no entry in `children`, so fall back to an empty list instead of reading `undefined`.
- Use an explicit stack: a chain of thousands of processes can be too deep for recursion in some languages.
- The root's parent is `0`, which is not a real process; it only appears as a key in the map.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `children` | map from a parent ID to the IDs of its direct children |
| `stack` | processes waiting to be stopped |
| `current` | the process being stopped now |
| `kids` | the direct children of `current` |
| `killed` | IDs of every process stopped so far |
